stations.title: Evaluate indications, urgency category, and obtain informed consent for emergency caesarean section
stations.prompt: A 26-year-old G2P1L1 at 39 weeks gestation with one prior caesarean section has been in active labour for 6 hours. For the last 4 hours her cervix has remained at 6 cm, the fetal head is at station minus 1 with severe caput, she reports persistent lower scar tenderness between contractions, and the CTG displays repetitive variable decelerations. Formulate the operative indication, determine the urgency category, explain the necessity of caesarean birth to the patient, and obtain informed surgical consent.
criticalItems: Establishes communication calmly and verifies maternal comprehension and capacity.
Clearly states the primary indication (cephalopelvic disproportion with arrest of progress) and warns of impending scar dehiscence.
Explains the four core surgical risks: bleeding requiring blood transfusion, infection, accidental injury to bladder or bowel, and implications for subsequent pregnancies.
Explicitly states that bilateral tubal sterilisation requires separate antepartum written consent and cannot be added urgently without prior documentation.

examinerQuestions.q: What urgency category applies to this scenario and what is your target decision-to-delivery interval?
examinerQuestions.a: This is a Category 2 emergency caesarean section (maternal or fetal compromise without immediate life threat), with an institutional audit benchmark of delivery within 75 minutes, although earlier delivery is preferred due to scar tenderness.

examinerQuestions.q: What specific intrauterine resuscitation steps would you institute while mobilising the operating theatre?
examinerQuestions.a: Position the woman in full left lateral tilt, discontinue any uterotonic infusions, administer an intravenous crystalloid fluid bolus, provide maternal supplemental oxygen if hypoxemic, and prepare tocolysis if uterine tachysystole is present.

examinerQuestions.q: What are the common and serious risks that must be outlined during emergency caesarean consent?
examinerQuestions.a: Common risks include post-operative wound pain, surgical site or uterine infection (2 to 7 percent), and transient neonatal respiratory distress. Serious risks include severe postpartum haemorrhage, blood transfusion, emergency hysterectomy (about 1 in 670), visceral bladder or bowel injury (about 1 in 1000), and venous thromboembolism.

stations.title: Demonstrate lower segment caesarean surgical steps, head delivery techniques, and angle haemostasis
stations.prompt: You are the primary obstetric surgeon performing an emergency lower segment caesarean section for a 26-year-old with cephalopelvic disproportion and failure of progress in the active first stage. Describe your surgical entry, lower uterine segment incision, techniques to deliver a deeply impacted fetal head, uterotonic administration, and layered repair of the hysterotomy.
criticalItems: Verifies that preoperative intravenous antibiotic prophylaxis (cefazolin 2 g IV) was given within 60 minutes before skin incision.
Identifies and reflects the uterovesical fold of peritoneum and mobilises the bladder inferiorly using a Doyen retractor.
Demonstrates recognised manoeuvres for delivering a deeply impacted head, such as the Patwardhan technique or reverse breech extraction.

Administers slow intravenous oxytocin (5 IU by slow intravenous injection) immediately following delivery of the infant and ensures complete placental removal before closing the uterine wound in two layers.

examinerQuestions.q: How would you handle an unexpected lateral extension of the uterine incision into the broad ligament?
examinerQuestions.a: Apply Green-Armytage or ring forceps to the bleeding edges for temporary haemostasis, exteriorise the uterus, identify the course of the ureter and uterine vessels, place an angle figure-of-eight or mattress suture just above the apex of the tear under direct visualisation, and call for senior obstetric surgical assistance.

examinerQuestions.q: Why is exteriorisation of the uterus versus in situ repair chosen, and what are its physiological effects?
examinerQuestions.a: Exteriorisation facilitates optimal visualisation of uterine wound angles, assessment of adnexa, and rapid closure of bleeding hysterotomy margins, but it may cause transient traction-induced vagal nausea, vomiting, and maternal hemodynamic fluctuation.

examinerQuestions.q: What postoperative measures promote enhanced recovery after caesarean surgery (ERAS)?
examinerQuestions.a: Early removal of the urinary catheter (at 6 to 12 hours), multimodal opioid-sparing analgesia, early oral intake of liquids and solids within hours of surgery, early ambulation, early uninterrupted skin-to-skin contact with breastfeeding, and thromboprophylaxis.

skill.caesarean.basics.title: Basics of caesarean section: indications, categories, and decision-to-delivery interval
skill.caesarean.basics.oneLine: Principles of caesarean delivery, classification into maternal, fetal, and obstetric indications, and the four urgency categories
skill.caesarean.basics.why: Caesarean delivery is among the most frequently performed major surgeries worldwide. Understanding its evidence-based indications, the four standard urgency categories, and the audit standards for decision-to-delivery intervals allows the clinician to balance maternal surgical risks against neonatal benefits and avoid unnecessary surgical morbidity.

teach.heading: Definition and clinical indications for caesarean section
teach.body:
Caesarean section is the operative birth of a baby, placenta, and membranes through incisions made in the abdominal wall (laparotomy) and uterine wall (hysterotomy).

Indications are broadly divided into absolute indications, where vaginal delivery is impossible or perilous (such as complete placenta praevia, severe contracted pelvis, or pelvic bone tumour), and relative indications, where vaginal birth is possible but carries elevated risk (such as dystocia, breech presentation, or prior caesarean scar).

teach.heading: Classification of urgency: the four Lucas categories

rows: Immediate threat to maternal or fetal life
Sustained bradycardia, cord prolapse, uterine rupture, massive abruption
Maternal or fetal compromise not immediately life-threatening
Failure to progress, pathological CTG, failed trial of scar
Requires early delivery without acute compromise
Prelabour rupture of membranes with prior scar, unstable diabetes
Elective delivery at a time suited to patient and staff
Planned repeat caesarean, elective breech, stable placenta praevia

teach.heading: The decision-to-delivery interval and clinical principles
teach.body:
The decision-to-delivery interval (DDI) is an institutional audit standard rather than a biological threshold. In Category 1 emergencies, the internationally accepted benchmark is delivery within 30 minutes, though every minute saved reduces fetal acidemia.

In Category 2 scenarios, a 75-minute interval allows thorough maternal evaluation, fluid loading, regional anaesthetic placement, and informed consent without adversely affecting neonatal outcomes.

probes.q: What is the recommended target decision-to-delivery interval for a Category 1 emergency caesarean section?
probes.a: The audit benchmark for a Category 1 emergency caesarean section is delivery of the infant within 30 minutes of making the decision.

probes.q: Why is an elective Category 4 caesarean section routinely scheduled at or after 39 weeks gestation rather than earlier?
probes.a: Scheduling elective caesarean birth at or after 39 completed weeks significantly reduces the incidence of neonatal respiratory morbidity, including transient tachypnoea of the newborn and respiratory distress syndrome, which is twice as frequent at 38 weeks.

rubric.text: Accurately categorises indications into absolute versus relative maternal, fetal, and obstetric causes.
Distinguishes the four Lucas urgency categories and cites appropriate audit decision-to-delivery intervals.
Explains the physiological justification for scheduling elective births at 39 completed weeks.

skill.caesarean.findings.title: Putting the caesarean indication and intrapartum picture together
skill.caesarean.findings.oneLine: Synthesizing maternal symptoms, cervical progress, fetal descent, CTG tracings, and scar findings to establish an operative indication
skill.caesarean.findings.why: Deciding on an operative delivery requires synthesizing multiple dynamic clinical findings. Misdiagnosing labour arrest can lead to premature surgical intervention, while missing true cephalopelvic disproportion or occult scar dehiscence leads to obstructed labour, uterine rupture, and perinatal asphyxia.

teach.heading: Recognising labour dystocia: arrest of dilatation and descent
teach.body:
Labour dystocia (failure to progress) is the leading indication for primary caesarean section. In the active first stage (from 5 cm dilatation), delay is identified when cervical dilatation is slower than expected or crosses the action line on a partograph.

Secondary arrest of dilatation is defined as no cervical change despite at least 4 hours of adequate contractions, or 6 hours when contractions are inadequate, with ruptured membranes in active labour. Arrest of descent is failure of the fetal head to advance during the second stage.

teach.heading: Clinical signs of cephalopelvic disproportion

rows: Head engaging, 0/5 to 2/5 palpable above brim
Head high and floating, 3/5 to 5/5 palpable above brim
Cervix thin, well-applied to presenting part
Cervix loose or thick, anterior lip oedematous and trapped
Marked progressive caput (+2 or +3) forming early

teach.heading: Recognising scar dehiscence versus true uterine rupture
teach.body:
In a woman undergoing trial of labour after caesarean (TOLAC), differentiation between scar dehiscence and rupture is crucial.

Dehiscence is an occult separation of the myometrial scar with intact visceral peritoneum; the mother and fetus remain stable.

True rupture involves disruption of all layers, typically presenting with continuous scar pain between contractions, fetal heart rate decelerations or bradycardia, vaginal bleeding, and recession of the presenting part.

probes.q: What physical signs on vaginal and abdominal examination strongly indicate cephalopelvic disproportion in active labour?
probes.a: Key signs include an unengaged fetal head with 3/5 or more palpable abdominally, secondary arrest of cervical dilatation despite adequate contractions, progressive formation of a large caput succedaneum, grade 3 severe overlapping cranial moulding, and an oedematous anterior cervical lip.

probes.q: What is the single most sensitive indicator of uterine scar dehiscence or rupture during a trial of labour?
probes.a: An abnormal fetal heart rate pattern, especially prolonged decelerations or acute fetal bradycardia, is the most consistent and sensitive early sign of uterine rupture, occurring in up to 70 percent of cases.

rubric.text: Correctly defines arrest of dilatation and arrest of descent according to standard intrapartum guidelines.
Identifies the combination of high presenting part, excessive caput, and severe cranial moulding as diagnostic of disproportion.
Recognises CTG decelerations and localised continuous scar pain as primary warning signs of scar failure.

skill.caesarean.summary.title: Clinical summary: structuring the caesarean delivery decision
skill.caesarean.summary.oneLine: Synthesizing the indication, urgency category, maternal-fetal risk balance, and surgical consent into an actionable operative plan
skill.caesarean.summary.why: A concise, structured clinical summary ensures multidisciplinary alignment among the obstetrician, anaesthetist, operating theatre nurse, and neonatal team before embarking on surgery. Summarising key patient factors prevents avoidable intraoperative surprises and ensures that consent is verified.

teach.heading: The core components of an operative obstetric summary
teach.body:
A comprehensive caesarean summary integrates five essential elements: patient parity and gestational age, current phase of labour, specific clinical indication, assigned urgency category (Category 1 to 4), and maternal surgical risk factors.

Surgical risk factors include prior pelvic operations, suspected adhesions, elevated BMI, abnormal placentation (placenta praevia or accreta), and known coagulation disorders.

teach.heading: Balancing maternal safety and neonatal benefit
teach.body:
Every operative decision requires conscious evaluation of the risk-benefit balance. In true cephalopelvic disproportion or fetal compromise, prompt caesarean section avoids stillbirth, birth trauma, hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy, and pelvic organ damage.

However, it carries operative risks: increased blood loss, wound infection, anaesthetic complications, and future implications such as uterine scar rupture and placenta accreta.

teach.heading: Informed consent and rapid communication under time pressure
teach.body:
Even in urgent emergencies, the clinician must communicate the rationale for surgery clearly and empathetically to the mother and her birth partner.

Confirm capacity, outline common and serious complications in plain terms, discuss alternatives where relevant, confirm whether tubal ligation has been separately consented, and record the discussion contemporaneously in the patient record.

probes.q: What five essential elements should be communicated in a structured handover before an emergency caesarean section?
probes.a: The five elements are maternal parity and gestational age, the precise indication for operative delivery, the urgency category (Category 1 to 4), fetal status on CTG, and specific maternal surgical risk factors including prior scars, blood crossmatch status, and allergies.

probes.q: Why must bilateral tubal ligation never be performed during an emergency caesarean section based solely on verbal intraoperative request?
probes.a: Bilateral tubal sterilisation is a permanent, irreversible procedure requiring unhurried antepartum counselling and written informed consent obtained well before labour. Decisions made under acute intrapartum stress carry high rates of subsequent regret and violate informed consent principles.

rubric.text: Constructs a concise operative handover incorporating parity, gestation, indication, urgency, and surgical risks.
Articulates both immediate neonatal benefits and long-term maternal surgical consequences.
Demonstrates adherence to legal and ethical requirements regarding informed consent and sterilisation.

skill.caesarean.differential.title: Differential diagnosis: evaluating indications, trial of labour, and alternatives
skill.caesarean.differential.oneLine: Differentiating true cephalopelvic disproportion from hypocontractility, assessing suitability for instrumental delivery, and ruling out acute catastrophes
skill.caesarean.differential.why: Before committing a woman to caesarean delivery, the clinician must exclude treatable hypocontractility that may respond to conservative measures, evaluate whether assisted vaginal birth is safely achievable, and rule out acute intrapartum emergencies such as complete uterine rupture or severe placental abruption.

teach.heading: True CPD versus hypocontractile uterine inertia
teach.body:
Before diagnosing cephalopelvic disproportion and scheduling surgical delivery, the clinician must distinguish mechanical obstruction from inadequate uterine action (hypotonic uterine inertia).

Hypocontractility is characterized by infrequent, weak contractions (< 3 contractions per 10 minutes, lasting < 40 seconds) without severe moulding; this may respond to amniotomy and cautious oxytocin titration in an unscarred uterus.

teach.heading: Caesarean section versus operative vaginal delivery

rows: Head high, above ischial spines (station -2 to 0)
Head deeply engaged, station +2 or at pelvic floor
High transverse, brow, or face mento-posterior
Direct occipito-anterior or low cavity rotation

teach.heading: Ruling out acute intrapartum catastrophes
teach.body:
In a patient in active labour with acute pain and fetal heart decelerations, differentiate dystocia from acute life-threatening catastrophes.

Complete uterine rupture presents with sudden cessation of contractions, loss of station, and shock. Severe placental abruption causes a tense, woody, tender uterus and dark bleeding. Cord prolapse reveals a palpable pulsating cord in the vagina, requiring immediate crash section.

probes.q: What essential prerequisite criteria must be fulfilled before considering an operative vaginal delivery rather than a caesarean section?
probes.a: Prerequisites include fully dilated cervix, ruptured membranes, head engaged at station plus 2 or lower, precise knowledge of fetal position, empty maternal bladder, adequate pelvic dimensions, adequate analgesia, informed consent, and operator competence.

probes.q: Why is oxytocin augmentation relatively contraindicated or used with extreme caution in a woman with a scarred uterus?
probes.a: Oxytocin hyperstimulation significantly increases intrauterine pressure and wall tension, elevating the risk of uterine scar rupture by three- to five-fold compared to spontaneous labour in a scarred uterus.

rubric.text: Distinguishes poor uterine contractions from true bony or soft-tissue mechanical cephalopelvic disproportion.
Applies standard prerequisites before deciding between instrumental vaginal birth and caesarean section.
Recognises clinical features of complete uterine rupture, placental abruption, and cord prolapse.

skill.ix.caesarean.workup.title: Pre-operative workup and intrapartum monitoring for caesarean section
skill.ix.caesarean.workup.oneLine: Essential pre-operative investigations, blood crossmatch, continuous cardiotocography, and ultrasound assessment of scar and placenta
skill.ix.caesarean.workup.why: A systematic preoperative workup optimises maternal stability, anticipates catastrophic hemorrhage, screens for viral infections, and ensures immediate readiness for regional anaesthesia and neonatal resuscitation.

teach.heading: Essential laboratory investigations for operative delivery

rows: Quantifies pre-existing anaemia; lower safety threshold for spinal anaesthesia without coagulopathy
ABO & RhD verified, 2 units PRBC crossmatched
Immediate transfusion readiness for obstetric haemorrhage
Excludes consumptive coagulopathy in abruption, sepsis, or pre-eclampsia
Universal precautions, prevention of mother-to-child vertical transmission

teach.heading: Intrapartum fetal surveillance: continuous CTG monitoring
teach.body:
Continuous electronic fetal monitoring is mandatory during trial of labour after caesarean or whenever fetal compromise is suspected.

Assess four features: baseline heart rate (normal 110 to 160 bpm), baseline variability (normal 5 to 25 bpm), presence of cycling accelerations, and decelerations.

Pathological CTG findings (prolonged bradycardia < 100 bpm or recurrent late decelerations) mandate immediate Category 1 or 2 surgical delivery.

teach.heading: Ultrasound evaluation of the lower segment scar and placental site
teach.body:
Antenatal and intrapartum ultrasound confirms fetal lie, presentation, estimated fetal weight, and amniotic fluid index.

In women with prior uterine surgery, scan localisation of the placenta is essential to rule out placenta praevia and morbidly adherent placenta accreta spectrum under the anterior scar.

A lower uterine segment full-thickness measurement under 2.0 to 2.5 mm warns of scar thinning and higher dehiscence risk.

probes.q: What minimum platelet count is generally accepted as safe for administering spinal anaesthesia for caesarean section?
probes.a: A platelet count of 75000 to 80000 per microlitre is generally considered the lower safety threshold for spinal anaesthesia in the absence of rapid consumption or coagulopathy.

probes.q: Why is ultrasound exclusion of placenta accreta spectrum vital before repeat caesarean section?
probes.a: An anterior low-lying placenta overlying a previous caesarean scar carries a high risk of placenta accreta spectrum, which can cause catastrophic peripartum hemorrhage requiring balloon tamponade, uterine artery embolisation, or emergency caesarean hysterectomy.

rubric.text: Selects and interprets haemoglobin, platelets, blood group crossmatching, and coagulation screens correctly.
Identifies pathological cardiotocography features warranting urgent surgical intervention.
Explains the significance of placental localisation and lower uterine segment scar thickness on ultrasound.

skill.annex.caesarean.robson.title: The Robson Ten-Group Classification System for caesarean delivery audit
skill.annex.caesarean.robson.oneLine: The World Health Organization standard 10-group classification system to monitor, audit, and compare caesarean delivery rates
skill.annex.caesarean.robson.why: The World Health Organization endorsed the Robson 10-group classification system as the global standard for auditing and comparing caesarean section rates. By categorising all deliveries based on readily available obstetric parameters, it identifies which patient groups drive institutional caesarean rates and targets quality improvement interventions.

teach.heading: Principles and variables of the Robson classification
teach.body: The Robson system classifies all admitted women into 10 mutually exclusive, completely inclusive groups based on five core obstetric characteristics: parity (nulliparous or multiparous), onset of labour (spontaneous, induced, or pre-labour caesarean), gestational age (preterm < 37 weeks or term >= 37 weeks), fetal presentation (cephalic, breech, or abnormal lie), and number of fetuses (single or multiple).

teach.heading: Robson Groups 1 through 5: term cephalic deliveries

rows: Reference cohort for intrapartum care quality; WHO sets no target rate for any group
Reflects induction of labour policies and primary elective CS rates
Multiparous (no prior CS), single cephalic, >= 37 wk
Usually the largest cohort; WHO sets no target rate for any group
Multiparous (no prior CS), single cephalic, >= 37 wk
Reflects medical induction protocols in multiparas without prior scar
Multiparous, at least one prior CS, single cephalic, >= 37 wk
Major driver of overall hospital CS rate; reflects VBAC uptake

teach.heading: Robson Groups 6 through 10: high-risk and malpresentation groups

rows: High CS rate (80 to 95 percent) post-Term Breech Trial
High CS rate (70 to 90 percent), selective vaginal breech birth
Variable (50 to 75 percent), dictated by presentation of twin A
Near 100 percent (absolute mechanical indication for caesarean)
All single cephalic, before 37 completed weeks (up to 36 weeks and 6 days)
Reflects management of preterm FGR, abruption, and severe pre-eclampsia

probes.q: Which Robson group is typically the largest contributor to the overall caesarean section rate in secondary and tertiary maternity hospitals?
probes.a: Robson Group 5 (multiparous women with at least one previous caesarean section, single cephalic pregnancy at term) is the single largest contributor to the overall caesarean rate in most hospitals.

probes.q: Why is Robson Group 1 considered the most critical group for evaluating quality of intrapartum obstetric care?
probes.a: Robson Group 1 consists of low-risk nulliparous women at term in spontaneous labour; primary caesarean section in this group converts a healthy woman into a scarred uterus for all future pregnancies.

rubric.text: Identifies the five core clinical parameters that define the Robson classification.
Explains how Group 5 drives institutional caesarean rates and the impact of VBAC.
Applies Robson groups to identify clinical cohorts with potential for safe caesarean rate reduction.

skill.caesarean.diagnosis.title: Diagnostic formulation, urgency stratification, and delivery plan
skill.caesarean.diagnosis.oneLine: Formulating a precise clinical diagnosis, categorising the urgency of delivery, and coordinating the multidisciplinary theatre pathway
skill.caesarean.diagnosis.why: Formulating a precise obstetric diagnosis articulates the primary surgical indication, establishes the urgency category, and communicates critical maternal-fetal factors to the multidisciplinary team to ensure safe and timely operative delivery.

teach.heading: The complete obstetric diagnosis formulation
teach.body:
A complete obstetric diagnosis formulation comprises seven essential elements: gravidity, parity, living children, precise gestational age in completed weeks, phase of labour (latent, active, or second stage), the primary surgical indication, and significant secondary complications.

Example: Gravida 2 Para 1 Living 1 at 39 weeks gestation in active first stage of labour with cephalopelvic disproportion, impending scar dehiscence, and non-reassuring fetal heart status.

teach.heading: Assigning the urgency category: Category 1 versus Category 2

rows: Acute bradycardia, cord prolapse, uterine rupture, massive hemorrhage
Rapid sequence general anaesthesia or fast spinal if indwelling epidural
Dystocia, secondary arrest, pathological CTG without acute crash
Prelabour rupture of membranes with prior scar, unstable diabetes
Planned repeat caesarean, placenta praevia, maternal choice

teach.heading: Multidisciplinary theatre mobilisation and surgical checklist
teach.body:
Once the caesarean decision is established, immediately activate the theatre multidisciplinary team: obstetric scrub nurse, duty anaesthetist, operating department practitioner, and paediatric resuscitation team.

Verify the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist: confirmed identity, signed informed consent, verified blood crossmatch, administered prophylactic antibiotics, and maternal left lateral tilt.

probes.q: What anaesthetic technique is generally preferred for a Category 2 emergency caesarean section and why?
probes.a: Regional spinal anaesthesia using heavy bupivacaine 0.5 percent is preferred because it avoids the risks of difficult tracheal intubation and gastric acid aspiration associated with general anaesthesia, allows the mother to remain awake, and minimises neonatal drug exposure.

probes.q: What specific intrauterine resuscitation manoeuvres should be instituted while preparing for an emergency caesarean for fetal distress?
probes.a: Manoeuvres include positioning the mother in full left lateral tilt to relieve aortocaval compression, discontinuing any oxytocic infusions, administering an intravenous crystalloid fluid bolus, providing facial oxygen if maternal hypoxia is present, and administering acute tocolysis (such as subcutaneous terbutaline) if uterine tachysystole is present.

rubric.text: Formulates an obstetric diagnosis incorporating parity, gestational age, labour stage, indication, and urgency.
Correctly assigns Category 1 versus Category 2 based on the immediacy of life threat.
Initiates timely intrauterine resuscitation manoeuvres while the operating theatre is being prepared.

skill.tx.caesarean.title: Surgical procedure, operative steps, complication management, and recovery
skill.tx.caesarean.oneLine: Step-by-step technique of lower segment caesarean section, management of difficult head delivery, angle extension haemostasis, and postoperative care
skill.tx.caesarean.why: Lower segment transverse caesarean section is the primary surgical delivery technique because incising the thinned lower uterine segment minimises operative blood loss, facilitates bladder reflection, reduces visceral adhesions, and provides an optimal myometrial healing site that carries a substantially lower rupture risk in subsequent pregnancies than classical vertical incisions.
skill.tx.caesarean.dosingNote: This module teaches management at the level of drug class and principle, quoting only the regimens as stated in the cited book and guideline sources below. All agents, doses, routes and regimens must be taken from your current national or institutional guideline at the time of prescribing. CliniX does not prescribe.

teach.heading: Preoperative preparation, surgical antibiotic prophylaxis, and incision
teach.body:
Administer surgical antibiotic prophylaxis with intravenous cefazolin (2 g IV, or clindamycin if penicillin-allergic) within 60 minutes prior to skin incision.

Position the patient on the operating table with a 15-degree left lateral tilt to prevent inferior vena cava compression.

Under regional spinal anaesthesia, prepare the abdomen with alcoholic chlorhexidine and perform a transverse suprapubic Pfannenstiel skin incision 2 to 3 cm above the symphysis pubis.

teach.heading: Abdominal wall entry and lower uterine segment hysterotomy
teach.body:
Incise the rectus sheath transversely and separate it bluntly and sharply from the underlying rectus abdominis muscles. Separate rectus muscles vertically along the linea alba.

Open the parietal peritoneum. Identify the loose uterovesical fold of peritoneum, incise it transversely, and reflect the urinary bladder inferiorly using a Doyen retractor.

Make a small 2 cm transverse curvilinear incision in the lower uterine segment and extend it bluntly with fingers or bandage scissors.

teach.heading: Delivery of the fetal head and difficult head extraction techniques
teach.body:
Rupture amniotic membranes if intact. Slide the right hand beneath the lower uterine segment incision below the fetal head, flexing the vertex and gently lifting it through the incision like a vectis while an assistant applies gentle transabdominal fundal pressure.

For a free-floating high head, apply Wrigley forceps. For a deeply engaged impacted head, utilise Patwardhan technique (delivering anterior shoulder first, then body, then head) or a sterile-gloved assistant pushing the head up vaginally.

teach.heading: Uterotonics, placental delivery, and two-layer hysterotomy closure
teach.body:
Immediately after delivery of the baby, double-clamp and cut the cord, and hand the infant to the neonatal team. Administer slow intravenous oxytocin (Syntocinon 5 IU by slow intravenous injection) to achieve vigorous uterine contraction.

Deliver the placenta completely by controlled cord traction. Grasp the uterine incision edges and lateral angles with Green-Armytage or Allis clamps.

Close the lower segment hysterotomy in two layers using synthetic absorbable suture (Vicryl 1).

teach.heading: Haemostasis, abdominal wall closure, and enhanced postoperative recovery
teach.body:
Inspect lateral uterine angles for extensions; ligate bleeding vessels. Non-closure of visceral and parietal peritoneum is standard practice and reduces operative time.

Verify complete surgical sponge, gauze, and instrument counts. Close the rectus sheath with continuous absorbable suture (Vicryl 1).

Close subcutaneous tissue if depth exceeds 2 cm, and reapproximate skin. Encourage early skin-to-skin contact, early oral fluids, early ambulation, and thromboprophylaxis.

probes.q: What is the recommended timing for administering prophylactic intravenous antibiotics for caesarean section?
probes.a: Prophylactic intravenous antibiotics, typically cefazolin 2 g IV, should be administered within 60 minutes prior to skin incision rather than after cord clamping, significantly reducing postoperative surgical site infection and endometritis.

probes.q: How is a deeply engaged, impacted fetal head managed during emergency caesarean section in second stage obstructed labour?
probes.a: Techniques include the push technique (a sterile-gloved assistant pushes the head upward from the vagina), the reverse breech extraction or pull technique (delivering the feet first through the hysterotomy), and the Patwardhan technique (delivering the shoulders and body before the head).

rubric.text: Specifies administration of IV antibiotic prophylaxis within 60 minutes prior to surgical skin incision.
Outlines abdominal entry in layers, uterovesical peritoneal reflection, and lower uterine segment transverse incision.
Describes recognised manoeuvres including Patwardhan and reverse breech extraction for deeply impacted fetal head.

cases.title: Sunita: 26-year-old at 39 weeks with previous caesarean in active labour with failure of descent and scar tenderness

patient.name: Sunita
patient.residence: District hospital catchment area, Nashik, Maharashtra; lives with husband and 3-year-old child

cases.opening: Doctor, this is my second pregnancy. My first baby was born by operation three years ago because he was bottom-down. I was hoping to deliver normally this time, but I have been having very strong pains since early morning, and for the past two hours the pains feel different, with constant severe burning over my old scar, and the midwife says the baby is not coming down.

skill.gen.appearance.finding: Alert, anxious, in visible distress during frequent labour contractions; comfortable between contractions until palpation of the lower abdomen; no pallor, icterus, cyanosis, or peripheral oedema.

skill.gen.vitals.finding: Pulse 92 beats per minute, regular, good volume; blood pressure 118/76 mmHg; respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute; temperature 37.0 degrees C; SpO2 98 percent on room air.

skill.exam.obg.preg_prep_inspect.finding: Abdomen distended corresponding to term gestation with longitudinal fetal ovoid; well-healed transverse suprapubic Pfannenstiel scar measuring approximately 11 cm; no visible peristalsis or Bandl retraction ring.

skill.exam.obg.fundal_height.finding: Symphysis-fundal height is 38 cm, corresponding with completed 39 weeks gestation; single fetus with clinically normal liquor volume.

skill.exam.obg.leopold.finding: Fundal grip reveals soft irregular breech; lateral grip reveals broad smooth back on maternal left and irregular small parts on right; first pelvic grip reveals hard rounded vertex high above pelvic brim; second pelvic grip confirms head is divergent and unengaged with 3/5 palpable above brim.

skill.exam.obg.fetal_heart.finding: Fetal heart rate is 142 beats per minute, regular between contractions, but auscultation immediately following contractions reveals transient slowing to 110 beats per minute with delayed recovery.

skill.exam.obg.fetal_diameters_station.finding: Head is in occipitotransverse position with parietal bone presenting; station is minus 1 (1 cm above ischial spines); significant caput succedaneum present (+2) with moderate moulding (+2) where parietal bones overlap but remain reducible on gentle pressure.

skill.exam.obg.pelvimetry.finding: Subpubic angle is approximately 85 degrees (narrowed); sacral promontory easily reached with diagonal conjugate estimated at 10.5 cm (reduced); ischial spines prominent and sacrosciatic notch narrowed, confirming borderline contracted pelvic inlet.

skill.exam.obg.labour_abdomen.finding: Uterine contractions are 4 in 10 minutes, lasting 45 to 50 seconds, moderate to strong intensity; distinct localized tenderness and pain elicited on gentle palpation over the left half of the lower segment scar between contractions.

skill.exam.obg.labour_pv.finding: Cervix is fully effaced, dilated to 6 cm (unchanged from assessment 4 hours ago); anterior cervical lip is oedematous and trapped against the pubic bone; membranes ruptured with lightly blood-tinged amniotic fluid without thick meconium; presenting vertex at station minus 1 with caput.

differentialModel.answer: Cephalopelvic disproportion with secondary arrest of labour in a patient with a previous lower segment caesarean section. Key differentials include impending uterine rupture or scar dehiscence, acute intrapartum fetal distress, deep transverse arrest, secondary uterine inertia, obstructed labour, chorioamnionitis, and complete uterine rupture.

accept: failed trial of labour after caesarean section
diagnosis.answer: Cephalopelvic disproportion with failure to progress in active labour and impending uterine scar dehiscence in a gravid woman with one previous lower segment caesarean section, requiring emergency Category 2 caesarean section.

managementModel.answer: Immediate emergency lower segment caesarean section (LSCS). Immediate resuscitation: discontinue any uterotonics, position in left lateral tilt, administer intravenous fluids and facial oxygen for intrauterine resuscitation, obtain urgent informed consent, crossmatch 2 units of packed red blood cells, administer preoperative antibiotic prophylaxis (intravenous cefazolin 2 g), alert the operating theatre, anaesthetic team, and neonatal resuscitation team, and perform lower segment transverse caesarean delivery.

teachingPoints: Trial of labour after caesarean (TOLAC) carries a 70 to 75 percent success rate in carefully selected women with one prior lower segment transverse incision, but requires continuous electronic fetal monitoring and immediate operative capability.

Secondary arrest of cervical dilatation (no cervical change despite at least 4 hours of adequate contractions, or 6 hours with inadequate contractions, with ruptured membranes) combined with high unengaged head, excessive caput, and severe moulding indicates cephalopelvic disproportion, mandating caesarean delivery rather than oxytocin augmentation.

Constant scar pain and localized tenderness between contractions in a scarred uterus is a cardinal red flag for impending uterine scar dehiscence or rupture. Oxytocics must be stopped immediately and urgent laparotomy performed.

The Lucas classification defines four urgency categories: Category 1 (crash delivery <= 30 minutes for acute life threat), Category 2 (urgent delivery <= 75 minutes for maternal/fetal compromise), Category 3 (scheduled during working hours), and Category 4 (elective at or after 39 weeks).

Surgical antibiotic prophylaxis with intravenous cefazolin (2 g IV) should be administered within 60 minutes prior to skin incision, and slow intravenous oxytocin (5 IU by slow intravenous injection) administered immediately following cord clamping to promote vigorous myometrial haemostasis.
